subsystems.name: Nanoparticle carrier
subsystems.role: encapsulates or binds the chemotherapy drug and determines how it moves through the body.

subsystems.name: Targeting layer
subsystems.role: recognises proteins found on cancer cells so the carrier sticks to tumours rather than healthy tissue.

subsystems.name: Stealth coating
subsystems.role: helps the carrier evade immune clearance and stay in circulation long enough to reach the tumour.

subsystems.name: Release mechanism
subsystems.role: triggers drug release only in the tumour environment, reducing damage elsewhere.

subsystems.name: Propulsion and control (true nanobots)
subsystems.role: moves the device actively and steers it, instead of relying on blood flow alone.

buildSteps.title: Choose carrier and drug
buildSteps.detail: Select a biocompatible material — lipid, polymer or inorganic — and a chemotherapy payload that can be encapsulated or chemically attached.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the nanoparticle core
buildSteps.detail: Use methods such as nanoprecipitation, emulsion or self-assembly to form particles typically 10–200 nanometres across.

buildSteps.title: Load the drug
buildSteps.detail: Dissolve or conjugate the drug into the core so that a large dose travels with each particle.

buildSteps.title: Attach targeting molecules
buildSteps.detail: Chemically link antibodies, peptides or aptamers to the surface that bind specific cancer markers.

buildSteps.title: Apply stealth coating
buildSteps.detail: Graft PEG or similar polymers onto the surface to slow immune recognition and prolong circulation.

buildSteps.title: Purify and characterise
buildSteps.detail: Remove free drug and unreacted chemicals, then measure size, charge, drug release profile and stability.

buildSteps.title: Test in cells and animals
buildSteps.detail: Check binding to cancer cells in culture, then measure tumour accumulation, efficacy and toxicity in animal models.

buildSteps.title: Scale up and sterilise
buildSteps.detail: Reproduce the formulation at clinical scale under sterile conditions, with batch-to-batch consistency.

prerequisites.why: decades of work on liposomes and polymer particles provide the basic toolkit.
many markers are known, but few are unique to tumours, so targeting is imperfect.
PEG coatings help, but repeat doses can trigger immune reactions and clearance.
only a small fraction of injected nanoparticles typically reaches the tumour.
true nanobots need engines and navigation that work inside the body, still lab-stage.

pathway.milestone: passive nanoparticle drugs such as liposomal doxorubicin and albumin-bound paclitaxel are approved and used in clinics
pathway.unlocks: reduced side effects compared with free drug, and a manufacturing base for nanomedicine.

pathway.milestone: actively targeted nanoparticles that bind cancer markers complete late-stage clinical trials
pathway.unlocks: higher tumour accumulation and lower off-target toxicity.

pathway.milestone: stimuli-responsive particles that release drug only in the tumour microenvironment
pathway.unlocks: precise dosing and less damage to healthy tissue.

pathway.milestone: autonomous or externally guided nanobots with propulsion and imaging feedback
pathway.unlocks: active search-and-treat capability, including hard-to-reach tumours.
